To clear up some points, as I've mentioned before, not everyone in Monaco is wealthy
One has to live in Monaco for more than three months a year and get a residence permit straight away . To maintain tax residency, in line with other countries, one needs to spend  a minimum of 183 days a year in Monaco.
Although, in theory, one should apply for a Carte de séjour after three months to continue to live in Monaco, in practise this is not always the case, and there are many that live in Monaco that do not have a Carte de séjour

replies.author: @monacophotographyevents2384
@monacophotographyevents2384
replies.text:
@UnseenWorldDocs_Us It's a combination of things..As I mentioned, there is virtually no crime here, in fact, the number one reason for arrest here is drink driving, it's impeccably clean, and there is a sense of community here. It's very international here and as it's such a small place many people know each other, and tend to hang out in the same places.
There is of course the lifestyle, but in general, day to day living here is pretty much the same as anywhere else in Europe.

It's worth mentioning that, although, obviously, one can live an expensive lifestyle here, it's possible to live here with limited amounts of money.
Rent for apartments, away from the main areas, isn't really any more than one would pay in any big cities, and prices for energy, phones etc are the same as in France.

Carrefour, the main supermarket here, is actually slightly cheaper than in Nice, and the people that shop there range from workers to the very rich, and indeed, they mingle, quite happily in the evening at various bars and restaurants.
It can also be cheaper to go out in the evening here to a bar, than in Nice..This is because, in France, 'happy hour' is illegal, but here it can go on for several hours.
There is a thriving night life here, which the people living here take full advantage of.

 I say people living here, meaning official residents, those that live here but are not officially resident, and the Monaco nationals (The Monégasque).

As I said previously, residents are happy to live here, and those that live here for tax reasons, can afford to live wherever they wish.
There is no shortage of people wishing to live here, there has been a rise in residents this year, and a rise in people applying for residency.

Did you know that there is a prison here? It was built in the 19th century during Monaco's economic growth, it's a remand prison that only has around 30 inmates in.,. It's below the Musée océanographique, and above the open air cinema.

Monaco, although not in the EU, follows EU laws and conventions, there is good social care here for the Monégasque that need it, in the form of benefits and social housing. And, of course, there is also universal health care here.
In fact, the Princess Grace hospital, which is a public hospital,is considered to be amongst the best in Europe.
Monaco also has the highest life expectancy in the world.

Of course, although the official languages here are French and Monégasque, by and large, the lingua franca here is English, followed by Italian. Many residents speak both English and French, but also many speak, French, Italian, English and their own language.

Monaco is not a tax haven, it is a country with favourable tax laws, and the banks and financial institutions here are governed by EU laws and regulations.
